title: Why Japan Is Stuck (and Still Rich Anyway)
note: EP037 — explainer (By the Numbers, row 27). Japan's paradox: 30+ years of near-zero growth, deflation, zero rates, zombie firms, aging + 250% debt — yet still one of the richest, safest societies on Earth. Real portraits (Abe, Kuroda). 5 new motifs (nikkeipeak, agingpyramid, debtownedinside, richbutstuck, zombiefirms) + doodles (torii, bullettrain). Target 12–15 min.

scenes.narration: Here's a riddle. One of the richest, safest, most advanced countries on Earth has an economy that has barely grown in thirty years. By the numbers, it looks stuck. By life on the ground, it looks wonderful.

Walk through Tokyo and you'll find spotless streets, bullet trains that are never late, long lifespans, and almost no crime. Yet economists have spent three decades calling this same country a cautionary tale.
It's one of the most misunderstood stories in all of economics. So let's untangle it — because Japan may be a preview of where the rest of the rich world is heading.
The textbook name for the stuck part is the Lost Decades — a lengthy period of economic stagnation in Japan that began when an asset bubble collapsed around 1990.

The sheer scale is hard to believe now. Flush with cash, Japanese firms bought up trophy assets worldwide — famously snapping up Rockefeller Center in New York, and paying record sums for Van Gogh paintings.
To understand the stagnation, you have to see the insane boom that came right before it.
scenes.heading: The Bubble

scenes.narration: Rewind to the 1980s. Japan was the economic miracle of the age — its cars, its electronics, its banks conquering the world. Many assumed it would soon overtake America entirely.
That confidence inflated the Japanese asset price bubble, where real estate and stock market prices were greatly inflated to staggering heights.

At the peak, the land under Tokyo was supposedly worth more than all the land in the entire state of California. The grounds of the Imperial Palace, more than all of California's real estate combined.

scenes.memeBottom: own the entire state of California
scenes.narration: On paper, the math had gone completely insane — and almost nobody at the time could bring themselves to call it a bubble.
The stock market went vertical too. The Nikkei 225 — the main index for the Tokyo Stock Exchange — nearly quadrupled in a few short years.
In December 1989, the Nikkei hit almost thirty-nine thousand. Everyone assumed it would keep climbing forever. Instead, that was the top — and it would not be seen again for thirty-four years.
scenes.caption: it took ~34 years to recover

scenes.narration: Then, in early 1992, the bubble burst. Stocks and land went into free fall. Trillions in paper wealth simply evaporated — and the hangover would last a generation.
And the banks made it worse. Instead of admitting their bad loans, they quietly rolled them over and pretended — a slow-motion denial that kept the sickness festering for years.
What followed has a name that still haunts economists: the Lost Decades.
scenes.heading: The Lost Decades

scenes.narration: Banks were buried under bad loans. Companies stopped investing. Shell-shocked households stopped spending and started hoarding cash. Growth flatlined — and stayed flat for decades.
And a strange new disease set in — one most modern economies had almost forgotten. Not rising prices, but falling ones. Deflation.
Deflation is a decrease in the general price level of goods and services. It sounds lovely — cheaper stuff! — but for an economy, it can be quietly poisonous.
Here's the trap. If prices keep falling, why buy today when it'll be cheaper next year? So people wait. Spending drops, businesses cut prices further, and the whole thing spirals downward.
scenes.caption: the deflation spiral

scenes.narration: Deflation also makes debt heavier. Your loan stays the same size, but your wages and prices shrink around it — so every debt quietly grows more crushing over time.
Japan's central bank eventually went even further — pushing interest rates below zero in 2016. Yes: you could effectively be charged to keep your money in the bank. Even that barely moved the needle.
So the central bank did the obvious thing — and discovered its tools had stopped working.
scenes.heading: The Zero Trap

scenes.narration: To fight a weak economy, a central bank cuts interest rates to make borrowing cheap. So the Bank of Japan cut… and cut… until it hit zero. And still, nothing moved.
This is a zero interest-rate policy — conditions with a very low nominal interest rate. Japan has lived here, on and off, for over two decades.
To fund all this, the Bank of Japan bought up bonds on a colossal scale. It now owns around half of all Japanese government debt — and became one of the biggest stock owners in the country, too.
But when rates are already zero and people still won't borrow or spend, the central bank is pushing on a string. Economists call this grim situation a liquidity trap.
Cheap money forever had a nasty side effect, too. It kept failing companies on life support — 'zombie firms' that should have died, but limped on, soaking up workers and capital.
A zombie firm earns just enough to pay the interest on its debts, but never enough to truly recover. Kept alive by near-zero rates, it quietly drags down the whole economy's productivity.
scenes.caption: zombie firms, alive on cheap debt

scenes.title: Japan's economy, 1989–2024
scenes.narration: Here's the whole arc. The 1989 peak. The 1992 crash. Zero rates by 1999. Abenomics in 2013. Below zero in 2016. And finally, in 2024, a new all-time high at last.
And underneath all of it runs the deepest force of all — one no interest rate can fix.
scenes.heading: The Demographics

scenes.narration: Japan has the highest proportion of people aged sixty-five and over of any major country — nearly a third of the entire population.
And the population isn't just old — it's shrinking. Fewer babies, almost no immigration, so each year there are fewer workers, fewer consumers, and more retirees to support.
scenes.caption: a shrinking, top-heavy population

scenes.narration: Other countries plug a labor gap with immigration. Japan has largely chosen not to, prizing social cohesion over population growth. It's a profound trade-off — and a big reason the shrinking is so steep.
Think about what that does to growth. An economy grows by having more workers, or more productive ones. Lose workers every year, and even standing still becomes a genuine achievement.
Instead, Japan leans on automation — more robots per worker than almost anywhere — and on getting more women and older people into the workforce, squeezing more output from fewer hands.
Now for the number that makes outsiders panic — and why they're mostly wrong to.
scenes.heading: The Debt Myth

scenes.narration: To prop up the economy for decades, the government borrowed enormously. Its gross government debt — the financial liabilities of the government sector — is the highest in the developed world.
Japan's government debt is around two hundred and fifty percent of its entire economy. For almost any other country, that would mean a catastrophic crisis.
And that scary headline number is gross debt. Japan's government also owns enormous assets, so its net debt is far lower. The truly frightening figure is, to a large degree, an accounting illusion.
So why hasn't Japan collapsed like Greece did? Because of who it owes. Japan borrows in its own currency, the yen — and most of that debt is owed to its own people and its own central bank.
That changes everything. There are no foreign creditors who can panic and flee. The debt is, in a sense, the nation quietly owing money to itself — and it can always print the yen to pay.
scenes.caption: huge debt — but owed to itself

scenes.memeBottom: a country that owes itself, in its own currency, is not Greece
scenes.narration: This is the single most misunderstood fact about Japan. Owing money to foreigners in a currency you can't print is dangerous. Owing it to yourself, in yen you control, simply is not the same beast.
Faced with all this, Japan launched one of the boldest economic experiments ever tried.
scenes.heading: Abenomics

scenes.label: SHINZO ABE
scenes.caption: Japan's longest-serving PM
scenes.narration: In 2012, Prime Minister Shinzo Abe launched a sweeping plan the world nicknamed 'Abenomics' — an all-out assault on deflation and stagnation.
Abenomics was the set of economic policies pursued by the Japanese government — built on 'three arrows': massive money printing, big government spending, and structural reform.

One arrow did fire hard: the weak yen. Cheap money made the currency tumble, which flattered exporters and the stock market — and powered a global 'carry trade' of borrowing cheap yen to invest elsewhere.

scenes.label: HARUHIKO KURODA
scenes.caption: fired the monetary 'bazooka'
scenes.narration: His central-bank chief, Haruhiko Kuroda, fired the first arrow with a monetary 'bazooka' — printing yen on a scale the world had never seen, even buying up stocks and bonds directly.
The results were mixed. It weakened the yen, lifted the stock market, and finally nudged prices up a little. But it never fully broke the deflationary mindset, and the debt only grew.

And then, recently, something shifted. After thirty years, real inflation and genuine wage rises finally returned. In 2024 the Nikkei smashed past its 1989 record — and the Bank of Japan cautiously began raising rates again.
So that's the 'stuck.' Now for the twist that the gloomy headlines always leave out.
scenes.heading: Still Rich Anyway

scenes.narration: Because here's what three decades of zero growth did NOT do: it did not make Japan poor. Not even close. Stagnation and poverty are two completely different things.
Japan still has a highly developed economy — one of the largest on Earth by total size, and genuinely wealthy per person.
So hold the two scorecards side by side. The economic spreadsheet looks bleak. The actual lived experience is one of the best on the planet. Both are completely true.
That's the real paradox. The growth chart is flat as a pancake — but the standard of living is sky-high. Stuck on the spreadsheet, rich in actual life.
scenes.caption: stuck on paper, rich in life

scenes.narration: Consider the scorecard. Near-universal healthcare. One of the longest life expectancies in the world. Low unemployment. Low inequality. World-class infrastructure. And streets so safe children ride the subway alone.

scenes.title: Life expectancy (years)
scenes.narration: Take life expectancy. People in Japan live longer than almost anyone on Earth — years beyond the United States. A 'failing' economy that quietly delivers some of the longest, healthiest lives in human history.
And on the world stage, Japan is no pauper. For years it was the planet's largest creditor nation — meaning the world, on net, owes money to Japan, not the other way around.
Here's the subtle trick the numbers hide. If your population is shrinking, then even a flat economy means a slowly rising slice of pie for each remaining person. Flat total, steady per head.

scenes.memeBottom: build a stable, rich, healthy society that stopped growing
scenes.narration: It forces an uncomfortable upgrade in how we think. Maybe endless growth was always the means — and a good, secure life was supposed to be the end.
Which raises the question that makes this whole story matter to you.
scenes.heading: The Canary
scenes.kicker: a preview of the rich world

scenes.narration: Japan isn't a freak. It's just early. Aging populations, falling birth rates, mountains of debt, and the limits of low interest rates are now arriving across the whole rich world.
And the queue behind Japan is long. South Korea, Italy, Germany, and even China are now aging and slowing in strikingly similar ways. Japan just got to the future first.
Europe, China, and even parts of the United States are starting to show the very same symptoms. Japan has simply been living in their future for thirty years already.
Which flips the lesson entirely. Maybe the question isn't 'what went wrong with Japan?' Maybe it's 'how did Japan stay this rich, safe, and stable while barely growing at all?'
Because our entire economic worldview assumes growth, forever. Japan quietly poses the heretical question: what if a mature, wealthy country simply… stops growing — and manages to be perfectly fine?
Economists even have a name for the idea Japan keeps bumping into: a 'steady-state' economy — one that stays roughly the same size, and focuses on living well rather than endlessly getting bigger.
So let's total up the paradox.
scenes.heading: The Final Math

scenes.narration: A giant bubble burst. Deflation and zero rates trapped the economy. An aging, shrinking population froze growth. Debt soared past two hundred percent. And yet — Japan stayed one of the best places on Earth to live.
The 'stuck' is real. The stagnation, the debt, the demographic cliff — none of it is a mirage. But neither is the wealth, the safety, or the extraordinary quality of everyday life.
Japan is proof that an economy can stop growing and not fall apart. Whether that's a warning or a quiet blueprint for an aging planet… may be the biggest economic question of our century.
So the next time you see a headline mocking Japan's 'stuck' economy, you'll know the other half of the story — the rich, stable life hiding behind that flat line.

youtube.hook: One of the richest, safest countries on Earth has barely grown in thirty years. This is Japan's paradox, by the numbers: the biggest asset bubble in history, the 1989 Nikkei peak that took 34 years to reclaim, the Lost Decades of deflation and zero interest rates, zombie firms, an aging and shrinking population, and a government debt near 250% of GDP — and yet a society that stayed wealthy, healthy, and remarkably stable. Why it's stuck, why it's still rich, and why it may be a preview of the whole aging rich world. Fully cited.
